utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor against -- versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone -- Mundis, and our case manager, Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. For General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Mr. Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, on Wednesday, the 20th of January, 2005 this is the 165th day of the trial. I wish to greet everyone in the courtroom, the counsel, the accused, and the witness in the courtroom, as well as all the personnel working in this courtroom. First, the Chamber will hand down its oral ruling on the admissibility of two exhibits. I will read out the ruling slowly in order to get the best possible interpretation. At the request of the Prosecution to have exhibits admitted in connection with the testimony of Ramo Durmis of the 26th of October, 1993 and the list of members of the El Mujahed Unit who left that unit on the 9th of February, 1994, the Trial Chamber pursuant to its oral ruling of the 29th of November, 2004 has decided that these two documents may be admitted as exhibits; however, they may only be used to test the credibility of the witness. Under these conditions, these documents cannot be marked only for identification. You will have an opportunity to read this oral decision as well. Now, Mr. Registrar, would you please assign numbers to these two exhibits with the proviso that has been mentioned in this decision.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The exhibit numbers will be as follows: The first document of the 26th of October, 1993, entitled "Record of interview of the accused Ramo Durmis," will be P941, and its translation into English, P941/E. The second document, of the 9th of February, 1994, entitled "List of foreign citizens who left the detachment," will be Exhibit number P942, and its translation into English will be P942/E. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar said that these documents were admitted with the proviso mentioned in the ruling, but this has not been entered into the record in English. The record has now been corrected. I must repeat that these two documents, P941 and P942, have been admitted exclusively within the restrictions of the oral decision handed down today. That is what was said in French but wasn't heard in English. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution at this point would simply alert the Chamber and the Defence to the possibility or to raise this issue now that our view would be that if we at a subsequent date bring additional witnesses or lead evidence concerning these documents, that we -- that the proviso would either be released or alternatively that the documents would be retendered into evidence for the purpose of establishing the truth of the matter contained in the documents. I simply want to put that on the record that that would be our position, depending, of course, upon future witnesses or future developments in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your position has been entered into the record. And now we shall resume the examination of this witness. It must be said, however, that yesterday there was some discussion in connection with two documents that were not disclosed. The Judges are still debating the matter, and we shall hand down an oral decision a little later. In connection with the problem raised by Mrs. Benjamin in the course of next week, we shall hand down a decision relating to the disclosure of documents before a hearing that the Defence wishes to use during the testimony of one of their witnesses. I now again give the floor to the Defence so that they can continue their examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. SAKIB ZIKO [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ziko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday at the end of the day we were mentioning the fact that Commander Hadzihasanovic, because of the extremely difficult combat situation in the Zepce [Realtime transcript read in error"Zepa"] area had -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, at that forward command post, were some of your colleagues from the operations and training organ also present? Were they working there, your colleagues from the operations centre, so that the commander could exercise his functions connected with the mission in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, did you personally work in that area? Did you go there in the period of July and August while there was a forward command post there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was part of the second group that replaced Mr. Vezir Jusufspahic, a colleague from the operative centre, and I continued on there almost until my return to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. In line 16, on page four it says: "Zepa," it should say: "Zepce." Yesterday you were shown three documents: One of the 30th June; one of the 9th of July; and 1 of the 11th of July about the situation in the area. Mr. Ziko, as you yourself were at the forward command post for a while, tell me, do these documents reflect the situation and the gravity of the situation facing the commander of the 3rd Corps in this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This partly illustrates the situation; however, the situation was so complex that it is hard to depict. But this document does illustrate it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ziko, did you have any information not only about fighting with the HVO? At that time, did the commander have any information and was it evident on the combat lines that the battle against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was being waged not only by the HVO? And if you have such information, tell me what forces were facing the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was then a union between the HVO and the Chetniks, and that part of the theatre of war which had previously been relatively quiet for the 3rd Corps, they opened up a new flashpoint. They expelled the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond population from Novi Seher, they cleansed the population from the river to Maglaj, from the River Bosna to Maglaj in the Zepce municipality, and they established their line on the dominant features facing the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel and witness please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Ziko, what were the forces at the disposal of the enemy at that time in relation to the units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the HVO units were partly armed with light weapons and some artillery, they didn't have any significant weapons until they joined up with the forces of the Serbian aggressor, where from the area of Ozren large forces came which were armoured and mechanised, and they had manpower as well as heavy artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of this overall situation in the area we are discussing, Mr. Ziko, tell me, for how -- or, rather, how much time, if any, did the commander have to devote to other issues in other parts of the territory of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As a rule, he didn't have any time for anything else. But he transferred some of his duties to his deputy, to the Chief of Staff, and all the officers from the command of the 3rd Corps. His priority was this area we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this connection, another question: As this area is to the north of Zenica, tell me, please, did the defence of that territory have any significance for the defence of the area of Northern and North-Eastern Bosnia, that is, the area around Tuzla and the area where there were about a million inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina and refugees? Was that area of any military and strategic significance for the survival of other parts of the free territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This territory was exceptionally significant for us in the Zenica region because of the road communications and because of the depth of the territory. For the aggressor, this would have meant cutting off all these communications and creating enclaves. For example, Maglaj, Tesanj, Zavidovici would have been in one enclave and Zenica in another. And we have had experience of the fate of enclaves, so I believe this would have been even more tragic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness a map. And with his assistance, could we mark the areas where combat activity was taking place and where Commander Hadzihasanovic's forward command post was located. This map is part of a series of maps that we have already tendered into evidence. This is set 2 in set Sarajevo and Doboj. The scale is 1 to 200.000. So this map was compiled on the basis of these maps that are in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We could perhaps place the map on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this map, Mr. Ziko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've always worked with maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please use this map to indicate the location of Zenica and the location of the headquarters of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica was on the N15 road from Zenica to Zepce, Maglaj, and Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put the map further up on the ELMO, because we can't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Or you could move the map. Please take a pencil and encircle "Zenica," mark that location with number "1".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenica, number 1, command post of the 3rd Corps. This is the wider area. So I couldn't find this exact point on the map. This is the Zepce sector; I'll mark it with number 2. The forward command post would be in the wider sector of Golubinja. In this case -- well, I'll mark it with an "X" here. That's number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using this map, would it be possible to point to the front lines, to indicate the front lines, or is this map not sufficiently accurate to indicate the lines facing the Serbian aggressor and the HVO? Apart from Zepce are there any other points you could indicate on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there is a large-scale map. We used maps, the scale of which was 1 to 50.000. And for reports to the Supreme Command Staff the scale was 1 to 100.000. For the units, the scale was 1 to 25.000 in order to be able to locate significant features. But I don't think I'll be very mistaken if I indicate the location of certain features on this map too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. It's not necessary, then. You said that this region was significant and that it was significant because other places that weren't involved in the combat around Zepce were also under threat. Could you encircle the place you have just been testifying about, in the north -- or, rather, north-east of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since Zavidovici is a large industrial area which is settled, if you cut off the road to Zepce and cut off the road towards Maglaj in this area, Zavidovici is then in a very awkward position, since that is the only good road that can be used for the rapid transport of people. And in this case, it concerned the inhabitants who were very often shelled and hit by Chetniks or fired at by Chetniks. So this road was very important for the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark "Zavidovici" with number "4".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the northern part of the map, there are some other places you have testified about, so could you please tell us something about them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Maglaj, and there is another feature here -- or, rather, this is a town which is separate. And there is Tesanj, which I will mark with number 6. Teslic was in the hands of the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. I'll mark a line here to indicate that Ozrenski part up until the conflict with the HVO. There was another line here. So this was a semi-enclave in the real sense of the term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please write down your first and last names on this map and the date today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, I would like to tender this map into evidence. And this concludes my examination-in-chief of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis -- Ms. Benjamin, any objections to this map being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will show the map to the Prosecution, the accused. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. DH1993 will be the exhibit number for the map, which has been marked by the witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does -- do Mr. Kubura's Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now turn to the Prosecution, who may commence with their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and along Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond with my colleague, we represent the Prosecution in this matter. I am going to ask you a few questions so as to clarify certain things for us. If, however, when I'm doing this you do not understand me clearly or you need me to rephrase the question in any way, please feel free to interrupt and I will oblige. Thanks. Yesterday my learned friend asked you a question in connection with the task that Commander Hadzihasanovic was faced with and assigned to when he came to Zenica. And according to page 82 of the transcript, line 4, you said that "a commander of a corps and of a larger unit knows what an operation unit is and what operations and training body is. And it's the commander's right hand; it's the commander's brain." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please elaborate for me when you said that the department of operations -- or the operations unit, rather, is the commander's right hand and the commander's brain. Could you please clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It would be logical for a commander, as the most responsible individual for the 3rd Corps, to receive all information, information which was insignificant and information which was significant for the corps command and for him to have contact with the lowest levels of contact, to have contact with other organs from the unit, and he wouldn't be in a position to be rested, to be functional in order to act in a productive way. The operations organ is an organ that gathers all information from all relevant elements, from civilian structures, from units, from the superior command, from the MUP on the situation in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and it's on the basis of this information that we, an operations organ, make proposals. So we are the brain that gathers all the information, and the commander is the person who makes a selection, decides on the importance to give certain information. In this way, we are an organ whose responsibility it is to inform the subordinate units on any omissions. This isn't the commander's responsibility. Otherwise, a commander would have to work for far longer hours, and I don't think he would be in a position to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to -- after listening to you, if I were to assess what you say in these terms, would I be right: That the commander's role was more of a rubber stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, since there's just one commander, all the others had to perform our own duties by making proposals when he was present. But when he was absent from the command post, we also took certain decisions for which we had competence. On a number of occasions, I said yesterday that the commander was frequently unable to read documents that came from the field. He had an operations and training organ. He had his assistants. He had staff, a Chief of Staff, a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in connection with your role as an officer in the training and operations department, could you clarify for the Trial Chamber whether your role was specifically in training officers to draft orders or your role expanded to more than that, your training role.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As a member of the operations and training organ, it was my responsibility - and this was the case for all other officers too who had experience in drafting orders - to participate in operations to draft orders. I and my colleagues in the organ could not draft orders that had to do with intelligence, logistics, finance, and other matters that we were not responsible for. But I must point out that our command and the command of units was composed of people who had volunteered for the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it's quite certain that almost 90 per cent of the members were not soldiers or not officers and they had no experience of working in an operations organ. They had no experience in drafting orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you indicated in a response to my learned friend that it was your obligation to train lower-ranking officers or at least give them instructions in order for their work to be as good as possible. Hence the reason why I asked the previous question, because the impression I got is that your role was to train officers how to write combat reports. Am I correct? One.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're quite right. The reports sent to us from units had to be unified. All the reports had to be identical. It depended on the situation and on the task, but it was necessary for us to receive such reports so that we could forward them -- forward the same reports to the Supreme Command Staff. In each report, the first item was "Intelligence and security." They had to inform us of the situation of the enemy and the zone of responsibility of the unit. So this was the case for all units. The second item was the situation in our units. They all provided information that was relative to their zone of responsibility. The third item could be "logistics." They would state their requests for technical equipment and materiel that they needed. So these are the items concerned and we trained all officers to provide their own information on the basis of these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I'm permitted, could you explain to us how this training was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. As a rule, we -- if we went to the commands of units, we would take working booklets with us and the officers would then enter information in those booklets on the deployment of their units in the zone of responsibility, on the deployment of their command and units in the zone they had been allocated, and we would then inform them in a timely manner about the significance of symbols on maps. In the case of -- in this case, there was artillery, tanks, and other items of relevance. There were minefields that our units had, that the enemy had. So we said that those people should inform us of the zone of responsibility that was under threat or inform us of the areas in which they required requests. When we were checking the situation, we wanted to be able to determine whether the zone was threatened and whether there was sufficient forces to defend a given area. Secondly, the officers who came to the 3rd Corps Command were officers we checked. We tried to see whether they were familiar with the situation in the zone of responsibility and to see whether we had received relevant and correct information in the corps, and we wanted to see the extent to which they were familiar with military terminology or though this terminology was not something they were very familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One of the other aspects of your tasks that you told us yesterday was to actually be on the ground. And my question to you then would be: Was this specifically in relation to the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. It's not sufficient to go to the command, examine these work booklets, and visit the command. On the other hand, at the forward defence lines, the situation observed might be quite different. There may be insufficient troops. Officers may be behaving arrogantly. Or the defence line might not be adequately arranged in relation to the aggressor's forward line. This would mean touring, visiting either from the right or the left side of the area of responsibility of the units. They had to tour the entire area of responsibility, depending on the security situation so as not to imperil the men on the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you told us that in order to carry out your work or when you were carrying out your work, you encountered certain difficulties. And one such difficulty was the lack of communication equipment. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. On our arrival in the Zenica area, we were duty-bound to establish a corps from scratch, and that was very difficult. We were given assistance in establishing the corps by officers from the Zenica Regional Staff. And although it may sound a bit strange, these officers were not very well received because outside the area of Zenica, we weren't well known and they were a bit envious because of our arrival. This process was very slow, the process of equipping the units, establishing the units, and so on. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the transmittal of the orders? Could you assist us in how you got the orders sent out to the different units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After signing orders, we transmitted them in all possible ways. Those who had packet communications -- we used packet communications to send orders to those who had them. If they were close to the command post, we used couriers exclusively. We used every means available, but we insisted that the orders be in writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correct in saying that you had a wide range of -- of ways in which you could communicate to the units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, that wouldn't be correct because the means of communication we had were outdated. Those were means used for training. They were very poor. But even had they been very good, we did not have sufficient generators and batteries to make use of them. Very often we would fail to receive information by means of communication but, rather, an officer would call us up on the telephone and this information was very scanty.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, Mr. President, could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 599, which is one of the documents shown to him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure what page it will be in your language, but it's page 2 of the English version, and I want you to look at the very bottom of the page, to the left-hand side. Do you see a little box at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the initials?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it's below the initials. Do you have a box below the initials and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- below the -- and below the signature of the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we are looking at the same thing, your box should say "Date, 30th of June, 1993," and then below that it should say "Processed by." And then there are a couple means by which the document can be transmitted. Are you seeing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I -- when I look at this, it seems to --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if my learned friends on the other side could offer some assistance. It doesn't seem to be on the B/C/S. I don't know if it's in another part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document which we probably printed out from the CD where we have the Prosecution documents, this part is really missing, so it might be a good idea to find it in the evidence. Because there is only something in handwriting here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would the registrar please hand me this document in B/C/S. In the document in B/C/S, we cannot see what you are referring to. Perhaps we should look for the original document, because the stamp, which has been translated into English, in the original document might perhaps be on the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have this document at hand?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. The document that I have in B/C/S is the same as the witness has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in this document, in B/C/S we do not have the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. President - and it's as I indicated - it may be at the back of the original, as you quite rightly said. And I suppose the original is lodged with the Court, P59 -- no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. The document that is lodged with the Court does not have a stamp on the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Then I, Mr. President, I'm told that the original would be with the Evidence Unit. And perhaps we will have to get same, if it's -- if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm told that -- I'm told by my learned colleague that it's going to take us some time before we might be able to acquire the original. And the question to the witness, I can just put it to him in -- in words and see if we can get an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps we can ask the witness the following: If an order were sent, would someone somewhere note down the date, the hour, and the means of communication used to transmit the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is the rule. That shows that a document was sent on to a unit and at what time. If there is a packet communication, then that would have to be noted down. Or if it was sent by courier, that would also have to be noted down. Those are the basic elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And to add to that, would the document state the different route that the order would have been sent? And when I say this, would it state whether it's going by electric -- electronic communication, teleprinter, telegram, telephone, radio relay wire, et cetera, would it say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In any case, from the lower-ranking units, we received reports as to when they had received the order. All the orders sent from the command of the 3rd Corps were always sent to the most responsible officer who was there. Usually either the commander or the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So that it is possible that a document could have been transmitted during your tenure by several different means, whether it be teleprinter, telegram, telephone, whatever? Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said that the system was -- there was lack of communication and there was a problem with the methods of conveying the -- conveying the information, do you think that would be quite accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is accurate. We had the greatest possible problems with means of communication. Had we had good communications, we would have known about every change in good time, not two or three days later when the changes had become even greater.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it seems to me - and pardon me if I'm not understanding you- it seems to me that you were exposed to several different means of -- of transmitting communication.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, we misunderstand one another. We did have several different means of communication. If a unit had a basic means of communication for their communications with the superior command, they did not have their own communications with their subordinate units, so that they used their means of communication they had with us only to communicate with us. But the units, especially the lower-ranking units I am speaking about - companies, platoons, and so on - they did not have their own means of communication. Is this -- does this reply to your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. Thank you. When you were again describing your task for which the majority of your examination-in-chief was, you said that only matters of high significance were conveyed to the Chief of Staff and then if he felt it necessary, he informed the commander. Could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us what you determine as matters of high significance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every piece of information relating to the situation on the part of the aggressor, that is, movements of the aggressor, combat activity by the aggressor, regrouping of the aggressor, or any other kind of combat activity they undertook in relation to the units of the 3rd Corps was significant information for the commander. On the basis of this information, if it was important, the commander was duty-bound to act according to his assessment of the situation, whether he would utilise reserve units, whether he would require certain activities to be undertaken, and so on and so forth. The information that was used for our daily work, falling within the competence of the various organs of the 3rd Corps, this was information that was not for the use of the commander. But this information also had "For the commander" noted on the top, because they were submitted by the commander of the lower-ranking unit, who would then say "for the commander" in the report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you -- would you say that information on the existence of foreigners in the units of the 3rd Corps, would you consider that as significant information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If someone transmitted this information to the security organ or the intelligence organ, those would be personal information for that level but it would have a certain significance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what significance it may have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the significance would be that the commander should bear in mind what kind of forces these were. Because in the area of responsibility of the corps, we needed every man; we needed every weapon; we needed everything we could have. And if these men or anyone else was there putting themselves at the disposal of the corps command, then they would be very welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today in response to a question from my learned friend you said that the commander did not have time for everything else -- anything and everything and that he transferred some of his duties to his deputy or to the Chief of Staff; is that correct? Would you agree with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct. Because every absence from the commander of the command post, if he went to a place from which he could communicate, there would be a gap in between where he could not communicate, and then the deputy or the Chief of Staff would have to take on his duties and he would gather information or make proposals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me then if I said in light of what you have said that the commander in that instance would have been fully appraised, and is usually fully appraised on what's going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If the commander was in an area which was a matter of priority, he, together with the officers who had gone with him and the officers who were there in the field, would take measures to deal with the problem so that the officers in the command, the deputy commander or the Chief of Staff, were then in a position to issue orders, and this is how it would have functioned until the commander returned. The commander would not have been aware of all the information, especially since we were sometimes not in contact with the commander for two or three hours. And in certain cases, it was necessary to act within five minutes or within an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But I -- I agree with you, but isn't the deputy's duty to report to his commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But it depends on whether he's in a position to report to him as far as information is concerned. For us soldiers, it's not logical for important information to be relayed over the phone or Motorola that the commander had on him. All such information waited until he returned to the command or these people took measures without waiting for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you'd agree with me, as you indicated earlier on, that the ones of significance he was certainly appraised of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they assessed that something was of importance and that he should be informed of it, they informed him. But quite frequently by the time a commander returned to the command post, his deputy or Chief of Staff -- well, very frequently they wouldn't see each other for a couple of days. As to when information was relayed and as to when the person who was to relay the information was to relay the information, well, this is another matter. I wouldn't be able to say whether someone relayed the information or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my final question to you has to do with administrative matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And if the witness can be shown Exhibit 271E, which was shown to him yesterday. And I hope this time it's on your copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's going to be the last page of the English version, which is page 2, and it's at the very bottom of the page above the word "stamp." And it's two initials, "JV" and "/VE" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber tell us what that means on the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All documents that were forwarded to subordinate units or to superior units contained certain basic elements. As far as administrative affairs are concerned, you have a heading, "The corps command." That was one element. Then there was information according to which it was the corps command, that it was a strictly confidential document, the place where the document was drafted is mentioned, and the date is mentioned. To the right of the heading, it says: "Defence of the secret. Strictly confidential." Documents were given various levels of importance. It also states that the document is being forwarded. It mentions the type of document, whether it's an order, a report, et cetera, or whether it's a -- an answer to some other document. Reference is also made to the person it is addressed to. The items are listed in the document which refer to tasks, duties, et cetera. At the back -- at the bottom of the document, you mentioned initials in order to know who drafted the document. In this case, it's the initials of the first person, "JV," and then we have initials of the person who typed the document. Since we have to monitor certain activities, this is the information that had to be contained. And we'd then forward the document to the addressee, and then there is the stamp and the signature. These are the elements contained in documents that were forwarded from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the drafter of the document, the draftsman, his initials alone would be borne on the document; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look below the initials, you would see a box and then you would see a stamp. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the stamp, you see a signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, below the stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could -- could you tell me, if you can, whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to recognise this signature. It's not General Hadzihasanovic's signature. This document could also have been signed by the person who drafted it, Vezir Jusufspahic is the person in this case. This is an internal document from the operations and training organ. It's a warning we issued stating that units should respect previous orders about sending information of interest to us in accordance with the rules that we had established, although these rules were dependent on the unit. This couldn't have been -- or this could be his signature. It could be the signature of the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander or of one of the officers. Mr. Hadzihasanovic has a very distinctive signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I ask you that -- ask you this: Once the signature is in the box, whoever's signature it is, is it to be taken that that particular person saw the order and signed the order? Is it to be interpreted that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. This is an internal document from the operations and training organ. Yesterday on a number of occasions I said that the commander was not in a position to sign a large number of documents. This is an internal document. And given the commander's authority, we used his name and his position. But we would sign the document or colleagues of ours who were competent for this would sign the document. We didn't have the right to put down our own names because after all it is the commander who was in a position of authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As an officer of training and operations, would you agree with me if I say to you that that in itself was a dangerous precedent, to have a -- to have had adopted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one could say so. Since we didn't have any prescribed rules from the Supreme Command Staff and later from the Main Staff. We had no rules, and that is why the procedure followed varied. I've just mentioned some elements that these documents have to contain: The commander's signature and everything else. Well, in other cases procedure varied. Had rules been established, perhaps things would have been different. But this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, I believe you will agree with me, if I say to you that once your signature is there or your name is there and the signature is underneath it, it's purported to be your document. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a document but the document is the document of the person who drafted it, not of the person who signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with you on that point, but that's a matter of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. President, this concludes the examination -- cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Defence counsel, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just a few. Re-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question put to you by my learned friend, you spoke at length about the work of your operations and training organ and about the work of the operations centre. You mentioned all the duties that you were involved in. Given the level of the corps commander, were you within your organ duty-bound to follow in your requests policies established by the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was our duty to act in this way. But since at the level of the corps command there were no established policies, no established procedure, given what the commander would request -- or what the commander would request was requested on the basis of his ideas. Ideas varied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Naturally this has to do with specific procedures that you discussed with my colleague. But with regard to what you were testifying about yesterday, sometimes you yourselves were not sufficiently trained -- your units were not sufficiently trained. What sort of policies did the corps commander pursue with regard to the need for officers and soldiers to be trained and was it your task to take specific and permanent measures in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was the second priority of the commander. The commander had to ensure that the officers were trained and that they could work independently. So each organ within the 3rd Corps Command at its own level had to train subordinates in units, in battalion, in brigades, in the operations group, et cetera. And even colleagues in the joint command had to do this to ensure professional military conduct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I have understood you the duties you were involved in, receiving information, analysing information, and relaying important information to the commander and drafting orders, I believe that these duties related to the commander's main task, his mission, combat tasks for defence and engaging units in combat. Is that the area that the operations and training organ was involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you drafted or since you prepared orders for combat action, tell me whether the commander had any clear policies that you had to follow, in terms of respecting orders, the law, and international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The commander issues tasks with regard to those items, and we followed his guidelines, and he was a man who was a very prominent person, educated, and he respected all these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone who wasn't a professional officer before the war or who was involved in defence before the war for a long period of time and also acted as an active officer in the war, tell me whether your experience, the experience that you have of how armies function, tell me whether you are aware of any situations not only in Europe but throughout the world in which a country before it had established an army of its own was attacked and created an army in wartime conditions and trained its army in wartime conditions. Are you familiar with such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At least, this is not something that has ever happened, given the -- my knowledge of history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My colleague asked you whether it was your duty to train men, and you said -- or rather, you answered the question. Tell me, since Commander Hadzihasanovic from November 1992 until the 1st of November, 1993 was the corps commander, if you now would look back to that period and at the attempts that he made together with yourself, what would you say about the results you managed to achieve in such a short period of time, in terms of creating an army and turning it into a professional and disciplined army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my answer might be a little unusual, but as far as General Hadzihasanovic is concerned, he is someone that the politicians did not like. He arrived in the Zenica area and no one liked him because many wanted to be in that command post and he was someone who wasn't supported by the politicians. He had no particular support from the parties, the political parties. The results he achieved in that area were above average, as far as creating the corps is concerned. As far as the defence of the population is concerned, his own population, because Zenica had a lot of religious buildings and members of various religions. And when Novi Seher and Zepce fell, he demonstrated his greatness, and all I can say is -- all I can do is thank this man for the time that I spent with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ziko. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a technical and military question I'd like to put to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you said that you formed this operations centre that functioned around the clock. This operations centre which functioned around the clock, was it far from the 3rd Corps Command or was it near the Main Staff and the deputy commander and commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operations centre was in the nuclear shelter of the building where the 3rd Corps Command was located. And as far as its functioning is concerned, I said yesterday that the officers or many of them had no training. It was an operations centre that didn't have all the equipment that an operations centre requires. So it worked around the clock, but this meant that it was necessary to be present in the offices. If people had no responsibilities, no duties, they could sleep or they could have a rest. But we in the operations centre and the communications centre, which functioned 24 hours, had the obligation of reacting at certain points in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this operations centre, were there any maps the scale of which was 1 to 50.000, 1 to 100.000? Could you tell us if there were any maps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had one map the scale of which was 1 to 200.000, and on the map of Bosnia and Herzegovina we indicated our zone of responsibility and partially the zones of responsibility of our adjacent units, the 6th Corps from Fojnica and the 2nd Corps near Vares. We wanted to monitor the situation in Sarajevo too, since it was encircled, and this was a map which didn't have much importance for the 3rd Corps Command, but it was important to be able to follow the situation in the battlefield. We also had map it is scale of which was 1 to 100.000. Our corps had a large zone of responsibility. And there were certain sections of zones of responsibility, operations groups within sections, and the scale of these maps was 100.000 and 50.000. But given the premises, we weren't able to place all these maps on the walls. We would take the maps out when needed and we would indicate the changes that occurred on a daily basis on these maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a map on which you could monitor in realtime the positions of your units from hour to hour as well as of the enemy units? Did something like this exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As our maps were 1 to 50.000 and 1 to 100.000, those are big sections in relation to the actual situation on the ground. We entered this data in approximately, roughly, so that from hour to hour yes, that could be done. But we did not immediately enter the information before it was verified. We didn't have enough maps to be able to waste them. We had foils on which we could inscribe this and then erase this as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In this office where the maps were, did the commander of the 3rd Corps, the Chief of Staff, or the deputy commander come in to look at the maps to see how the situation was developing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corps commander rarely [Realtime transcript read in error "really"] came to the operations centre, but as the operations organ we were duty-bound to go to a map he had in his office from time to time and enter information that was of importance for him. The map of the intelligence organ, which was of special interest for the commander when it came to the deployment of enemy forces was separate, and this was in the office of the intelligence organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there is a misinterpretation, 31, 16. The witness said that "the commander rarely came." Here it says "the commander really came." Could this be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. Does the Prosecution have any questions to put arising from the questions on the maps?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for coming to testify about the events that took place and your activities in the 3rd Corps. On behalf of the Chamber, I wish you a safe return to your country. Now I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom so that you can catch your plane very quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence, please tender your exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we wish to tender document under tab 2, 1194, and to have the document in tab 7, 1397, which is only in B/C/S and goes to the facts that the witness testified about as to when he left the 3rd Corps, I ask that it be marked for identification only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are asking me for the admission of two documents, document 1194, which has been translated, and the one under tab 7, 1397, which has no translation, which would only be marked for identification. What does the Prosecution have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objections, but I think there may be a little error. The document DH1298, my friend has indicated that it -- it was already in evidence, tendered, but our records are showing that it was not tendered. Are we correct? DH1298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please let us first resolve the issue of document DH1298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar says that this document has been admitted. It was admitted during the testimony of another witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1298. Mr. Registrar, would you please assign numbers to these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The documents will be DH1194 and DH1194/E. As for the other document, it will be marked for identification as DH1397 ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is almost time for our break, so this is a convenient time. We have time until 13.45. When we return, the witness will already be in the courtroom. We will gain a few minutes in this manner. And then we shall continue with the last witness for this week. We shall resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. First of all, I wish to check whether you can hear the interpretation of what I am saying. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called as a witness for the Defence. Before you make the solemn declaration, you must introduce yourself. Tell us your first and last name and your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zaim Kablar. I was born on the 29th of June, 1957 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation? Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am employed in the Federal Commission for the Search for Missing Persons in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, were you holding any post or were you part of any military unit? And if so, what unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and the first half of 1993, I had a work obligation in the factory in which I was working in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were never part of the ranks of any military formation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up to the 25th of August, 1993, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you ever testified before an international or national court about the events in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in October 1998 before this Tribunal in the Kupreskic et al. case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you then a witness for the Defence or for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at that time, did you testify without any protective measures in public session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now ask you to read out the solemn declaration being handed to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I hear the interpreter better? The voice of the Judge is too loud in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usher is trying to solve the situation. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If it's better now, perhaps before I give the floor to the Defence, which will start examining you, to give you some explanation as to the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have already testified in another trial, this situation will not be completely unfamiliar to you. First, you will be examined by the Defence. You will have met the Defence counsel previously. After this stage of the proceedings is over, you will be examined or, rather, cross-examined by the Prosecution. After this stage, the Defence will have another opportunity to -- to examine you in their redirect. And the three-member Trial Chamber may put questions to you at any point; although, the Chamber prefers to do so after both sides have completed their examination in order to clarify any points arising from your testimony or anything else that they feel is in the interests of justice and establishing the truth. Please try to make your answers as full as possible. We have no written documents to accompany your testimony. What you say will be taken down. Before you on the monitor, you can see the transcript in English. I also wish to draw your attention to two points, which I make to all witnesses: First of all, you have made the solemn declaration to speak the truth. This excludes the possibility of making a false statement. Secondly, although this may not refer to you, I still wish to say it: The witness does have the right not to answer a question if he or she feels that answer may one day be used against them. In that case, which is very rare, the Trial Chamber may order the witness to respond to the question but will then give him a certain immunity. This is the way in which today's proceedings will -- will take place. And we will stay here until 45 minutes past 1.00. The Defence has promised that they will do everything in their power to complete your testimony today. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kablar.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell Their Honours something about your education, when and where you completed your education, and where you worked before the war.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I completed the secondary school for economics in 1976 in Travnik, and I was employed from 1976 until the 16th of April, 1993 in a company called Sintevit Vitez. This is a company within the Slobodan Princip Seljo group. That was a factory in Vitez dealing with the production of explosives, gunpowder, and I worked in another department which dealt in the processing of plastics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that in 1992 until -- until mid-1993 you had a work obligation. First of all, tell me, what town did you live in and did there come a time when this obligation ceased and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, tell me in what town you were working in 1992 and part of 1993. That's the first part of the question. The second part is: As you mentioned the 16th of April as the date until which you worked, can you tell me why your work obligation stopped.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I lived and worked in Vitez. Up to the 16th of April, when the conflict between the army and the HVO began, I worked there. And then three days later I was brought in and incarcerated in the Vitez cinema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this imprisonment, were you exchanged at some point?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I was conditionally speaking released when all the prisons were disbanded. It was on the 30th of April or the 1st of May. I'm not sure. And this was done unilaterally. And speaking conditionally, all the centres or camps or whatever they're called, these places, but not all of them in Vitez were disbanded. There were still prisoners left there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When asked by the President of the Chamber, you said that you did not belong to any military units until the 25th of August, 1993. Can you tell Their Honours where you were after the 25th of August until the end of war, or more precisely, until the end of 1993? That's the period we're interested in.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: On the 25th of August, 1993, I was appointed deputy of the president of the commission for the exchange of prisoners of the 3rd Corps, or more precisely, we were looking after prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what sector of the command of the 3rd Corps was your commission for the care of imprisoned members of the army?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: This was called the PK for morale and for religious issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the deputy president of the commission before you were and who was the president of the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: I was appointed instead of Beba Salko, and the president of the commission was Emira Bolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you took up your duty in the commission for the care of imprisoned members of the army, do you know whether there were any rules existing in the corps as to how prisoners of war were to be treated or rules pursuant to which you carried out your tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We had an instruction on the work of the commission for the care of prisoners of war. The commission was formed on the 5th of April, 1993 pursuant to an order from the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Before that, no one dealt with the problem of imprisoned members of the army. And the instruction contained details as to who was to do what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that before that there was no military commission in existence. Do you know whether there were any other commissions dealing with the exchange of prisoners of war and their status?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: There was a state commission and within the framework of this commission there were regional and municipal commissions dealing with these problems, that is, the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the framework of these instructions and your tasks in the 3rd Corps, where were imprisoned members of the enemy forces kept? Was a certain place designated where these prisoners had to be brought and from which you could carry out your tasks of exchanging them?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: All persons that were imprisoned were in the centre for prisoners of war in Zenica and only the commission for exchange of the 3rd corps had these prisoners at their disposal, and these were the only ones that we negotiated about and exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you arrived there on the 25th of August, 1993, tell me whether the subordinate units encountered any difficulties and were you yourself able to observe difficulties as far as implementing that order is concerned, the order according to which captured prisoners should be moved to the prisoner centre as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, you know that the 3rd Corps Command was in Zenica and the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps was vast. A unit that has captured an enemy soldier was not in a position to transfer the arrested men on the same day. They were transferred when conditions made this possible. They were transferred to this prisoner collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in the commission, was there a system in accordance with those instructions in existence for the corps and its subordinate units to deal with issues that concerned care for prisoners? Which organs were responsible for this issue in the corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: It was the sector for morale responsible for these issues, for the issue of the prisoners. All the brigades in the 3rd Corps had one army member each which assisted the 3rd Corps commission. He represented the brigades to take care of the missing members of the 3rd Corps and of the dead and to inform the 3rd Corps about this. These people who represented the 3rd Corps were also members of the Sector for Morale. So this was a system in place for obtaining information. These individuals in the brigade could negotiate with the enemy side but they couldn't get involved in an exchange without our agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what importance was it for you and the commission to obtain full and timely information from units in the field on the number of army members arrested, and is this the basis on which you negotiated with the other side?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Yes, that was the basis. If you have information at all the times, if you know about the losses sustained, if you know about the soldiers captured, well, then you would know how many soldiers were missing. If a unit had arrested someone, we had that information. But this -- this soldier might not be transferred immediately. It was not technically possible. But we had the information. But in negotiations if you acted immediately, it was possible for the soldier to remain alive. This was more difficult if he remained in the unit for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kablar, tell me, did operative groups in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps have a certain role as far as performing the duties that you had in the 3rd Corps Command are concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: For a certain period of time, the OGs also had a commission, a three-member commission, which was also involved in negotiations, but it could not carry out exchanges without the agreement of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When subordinate units engaged negotiations or established lists for possible exchanges for our side and for the enemy side, tell me, in such cases what sort of duties does your commission or the corps -- the 3rd Corps Command have in order to carry out the exchange?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps Command and I -- or rather, the 3rd Corps commission would make proposals, would suggest that a cease-fire be implemented so that an exchange could take place in no man's land, but it was necessary to receive authorisation to release prisoners of war from the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If criminal proceedings had been instituted against a prisoner of war, was this part of your responsibilities? And if the other side requested that he be exchanged, can you say what you had to do before you could become involved in the exchange of such an individual.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: We cooperated with the regional commission for the exchange of prisoners in Zenica very well, and if there was a person against whom proceedings had been instituted or if a person had been convicted, he was the responsibility of the civilian authorities. Then at the request of the regional commission, you would ask for approval from the state commission and authorisation could also be obtained from the Presidency of the BH. When there was a decision on a pardon or something of that kind, then one would get involved in exchanging that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kablar, tell me whether you also came across problems of any other kind that related to your work and to the work of state commissions at all levels, municipal, regional, and state levels. Were there any problems for which you had to violate that rule according to which you should exchange a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: When I arrived on the scene, I had many problems. There were a lot of prisoners in Zepce, over a thousand --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me who was imprisoned in Zepce.

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Civilians, troops, ABiH members. They had been arrested by the HVO. And all the families - there were over 1.000 men -- 1.000 individuals imprisoned in Zepce - and all these families, women and children, came to Zenica and they exerted continuous pressure on us to get them exchanged. And in the centre for prisoners of war, we had 30 individuals, and it was very difficult to work at the time. Then the HVO commission asked for families of Croatian nationality in Zenica to be linked up, and then through municipal commissions we bypassed our mandate. When we exchanged prisoners of war, we also included civilians. So in a certain sense, we did not respect the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on your final lists, it was possible to find individuals who were not prisoners of war. Could you clarify this? How is it that these individuals appeared in Zenica or in other areas under the 3rd Corps and how is it that these individuals were requested by the HVO in order to rejoin families?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Well, the HVO, when it left its combat positions around Zenica, they moved on their own with their weapons. Their families remained in Zenica. They were requesting that these families be linked up or if someone had joined the HVO in Zepce, that person might request to be linked up with his family from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these individuals who were requested to be joined up with their families for whom you weren't responsible? Who were these individuals, as far as the HVO were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: They were their wives and children, more distant relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived in the commission on the 25th of August. Had you participated in conversations with the HVO or representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska with regard to the exchange of our soldiers or of wounded or dead men in their area? Tell me, in those discussions, were representatives of the International Community usually present and who were they?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: In 1993, in the second half of 1993, most meetings were attended by European monitors, representatives of the International Red Cross with their headquarters in Zenica, the regional commission, the military commission, and the -- the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kablar, tell me, from the time you assumed your duties up until -- from the 25th of August up until the end of 1993, at the meetings that you attended was the subject of exchanging prisoners -- Mujahedin prisoners or killed Mujahedin prisoners discussed? Were you ever present at a meeting at which you raised such an issue or at which someone else raised such an issue?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me whether at that time when you assumed your duties from the 25th of August, 1993 up until the end of 1993, did the HVO at any time or any of the representatives of the International Community who attended the meeting ask about the music school, about the prisoners in the music school --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hate to interrupt my learned colleague, but the interpreter noted that the answer to the previous question was not recorded or was inaudible. I just draw that to her attention. She just may want to revisit that issue before moving on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I also see that the interpreters didn't hear the answer, so I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kablar, could you please tell me: From the 25th of August, when you arrived in the commission for taking care of the prisoners of the army up until the end of 1993, at the meetings that you attended did anyone ever raise the issue of exchanging foreign combatants, the so-called Mujahedin, either combatants who were alive or who had been killed? Did you ever attend such a meeting in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Not in 1993 but in 1994, yes, if that's what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now wanted to ask you whether during this same period of time, from the 25th of August, 1993 until the end of 1993, did any representatives of the HVO, of the International Community in the course of those meetings or in any other way raise an issue with the commission that concerned the prisoners in the Zenica Music School or that concerned the exchange of the individuals allegedly detained in the music school?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: Of all the negotiations that I participated in, this issue was never raised because all the prisoners were in the collections centre for prisoners. There were negotiations -- traditional negotiations about the exchange of prisoners and we used lists. We were provided a list from the HVO. The HVO would provide a list to us and we would discuss these lists. The music school was never mentioned nor any other locations -- other locations were mentioned but the music school was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the prisoners were in the centre for prisoners of war, as you said - and the Judges are already aware of the fact that that was in the KP Dom - can you tell me whether at any point in time you received from representatives of the international community complaints about the way that prisoners of war were treated in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: ZAIM KABLAR
utterances.text: No. I've already said that the NKCK headquarters was in Zenica and they were able to visit the collection centre for prisoners at any point in time in Zenica. That's where the ICRC and -- the ICRC was located. That's where the ICRC was located.
